messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard deviation (standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis is  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.2215 .
\]

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That might refer to the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Usually we compute the standard error: sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That is sigma/sqrt(n). But they gave sample standard deviation 1.4. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) = 1.4 / 6.3249 = 0.2215 approx.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/n) * (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). Actually the t-statistic is (sample_mean - population_mean) / (sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size)). The denominator is the standard error. The t-statistic has a t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom. The standard deviation of a t-distribution with df degrees of freedom is sqrt(df/(df-2)) for df > 2. So for df=39, the standard deviation of the t-distribution is sqrt(39/(39-2)) = sqrt(39/37) = sqrt(1.05405) = 1.0268. But the user might just want the standard error.
